consensus_summary: The consensus takes the primary and settled meaning of the great fish (Jonah) as a type of the grave/Sheol and of Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection (the sign of Jonah), the fish serving as God’s appointed instrument of judgment and deliverance; sea-monsters more broadly symbolize chaos/evil powers or hostile empires/nations (Pharaoh, Babylon), while ordinary fish can symbolize Christ or the church; the two image-sets are kept distinct.
book_summary: The book identifies the great fish/sea-monster as a great ruler among the sea of peoples—the personal head who stands for the kingdom, state, and administration acting through him—who swallows (through the body he heads) and is forced to give back what was swallowed (examples: Pharaoh/Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar/Babylon, Caesar/Rome).
consensus_core_identification: type of the grave/Sheol prefiguring Christ’s three-day burial and resurrection (Jonah’s fish as divine instrument)
book_core_identification: great ruler / personal head of a kingdom-state who swallows peoples and is forced to disgorge them
boundary_disagreement: Consensus keeps Jonah’s great fish (non-hostile instrument/type of tomb) distinct from OT sea-monster texts (chaos or empires); book unifies the combined term under the single political-ruler referent drawn from the empire-monster verses and extends it to Caesar/Rome.
material_contradiction: The book’s core referent (great ruler/kingdom head) replaces the consensus primary referent (grave / sign of Jonah for Christ’s entombment); the two cannot serve as the same central identification of the term in the same sense.
rationale: All consensus responses fix the primary, settled Christian meaning of the great fish on the Matthean sign-of-Jonah typology (belly = Sheol/grave). Empire and chaos readings appear only as alternatives, mainly for distinct sea-monster vocabulary, and mainstream notes explicitly decline to equate Jonah’s fish with Leviathan-type creatures. The book instead places the ruler-who-swallows identification in the entry proper (supported by the empire texts), while demoting the typology to a “commonly taught” note plus cross-reference. This is replacement of the central referent, not a boundary adjustment of the same referent, and therefore divergent.
strongest_objection: Jesus’ own interpretation (Matt 12:40) fixes the great fish as the “heart of the earth,” so any political-ruler reading must either subordinate or re-explain that dominical saying; the entry alone appears to displace rather than incorporate the NT primary sense.
